weeks.title: Alignment via Written Principles
weeks.description: This week, we discuss how AI models are aligned via written principles and guidelines, also known as model constitutions or model specs. We begin by studying the technical underpinnings of constitutional AI and deliberative alignment, two approaches pioneered by Anthropic and OpenAI respectively. We discuss how these approaches shape model behavior and also discuss the extent to which they’re effective. We later read excerpts from Anthropic’s Claude Constitution and OpenAI’s Model Spec and analyze their different approaches, including their philosophical implications on AI. We conclude with research that explores how effective deliberative alignment is in preventing scheming. The goal of this week is to understand what model constitutions/specs are, learn how they are trained into models, and form opinions on how they should be constructed.

articles.title: Recent Developments in AI
articles.html:
Gemini 4 Argon and Muse Wonder released

Google announced Gemini 4 Argon on September 30, 2026. Google reported that Gemini 4 Argon achieves 77.9% on DeepSWE v1.1 and 68% on CWE-bench v1, which indicates coding and cyber capabilities at or near the frontier. For safety purposes, Google has initially released Gemini 4 Argon only to trusted cyber defenders.

Meta released Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full on October 12, 2026. Initial benchmark reporting also points to near-frontier capabilities. Meta emphasizes agents that can sustain work across apps and retain relevant context.

Scores on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index over time for models by each of the five major US AI labs. The Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index is a composite evaluation that aggregates scores across many diverse benchmarks. Each dot represents a new high score for a lab. Open circles are estimated scores.

Sources: Google announcement (Sep 30); Meta research release and benchmarks (Oct 12); Artificial Analysis leaderboard and methodology (retrieved Oct 12).

OpenAI fires three safety employees

In early October, OpenAI fired three of its AI safety researchers: Tomek Korbak, Jasmine Wang and Mikita Balesni. OpenAI claimed that the researchers had “violated clear policies on handling sensitive information”, but remained vague about what constituted the violation. It is speculated that the violations were related to information leaks about new less-monitorable architecture, or about the researchers’ contacts with METR during the Hugging Face incident investigation. The researchers deny these allegations and say their outside contact was part of their jobs. Previously, Korbak had worked on chain-of-thought monitorability and was OpenAI’s main contact with METR during the Hugging Face incident investigation, Balesni had led cross-company coordination efforts to prevent labs from developing less monitorable architectures, and Wang had co-led the safety cases program. In an open letter to OpenAI’s safety oversight groups, the three expressed worries that their firings would make remaining staff afraid to raise safety concerns, which would weaken OpenAI’s alleged culture of open debate and transparency. They also urged OpenAI not to use their firings as an excuse to scale back its work with outside auditors like METR. OpenAI denied the firings were about raising safety concerns, and said it is finalizing contracts with outside safety assessors.


Three safety and alignment employees were fired by OpenAI on October 1, 2026. From left to right, Mikita Balesni, Jasmine Wang, and Tomek Korbak.

Sources: Open Letter; OpenAI response; APNews
